text: Describe a small 3D scene as JSON and get a flat SVG picture of it from any angle. Inspired by Zdog . Pronounced "zee-pup". These four pictures come from one scene : eleven solids with one color each, plus a door and a window, placed in 3D. Only the view angle differs. Zpup works out what hides what and how each face is shaded, and writes a plain SVG with no JavaScript, so the picture works in an tag, an email or a README. One view of the lighthouse is 5.5 KB. Try it in the playground : edit a scene as JSON, drag the picture to turn it, and export the SVG. Both halves are the same solids at the same places and sizes ( Zdog script , Zpup scene ); the Zdog half is a flip-book of Zdog's own SVG output, one frame every 3 degrees. Watch the hut and the boulder as they pass behind the tower: in Zdog the island is painted over them. Zdog orders shapes by one point each, so a large shape such as the ground covers smaller ones that sit on it once they are farther away than its center. In Zdog the fix is done by hand, with groups or by cutting the large shape up. Zpup compares every pair of shapes that overlap on screen and works out which one is in front. In the benchmark , the median share of a picture painted in the wrong order was 2.9% and 4.2% for Zdog in two runs, and 0.4% and 0.3% for Zpup. Small illustrations with volume: icons, mascots, props, a little building. The scene is data, so a person, a script or an AI model can write it, and mistakes come back as errors that say where and how to fix them. Each picture links to its scene, 60 to 150 lines of TypeScript. The cactus uses soft shading . It is not a 3D engine. There is no perspective, no textures and no light to place, and shapes that cut deep into each other are not drawn correctly. There is no text shape and no clipping either. For that, use three.js or a modeling tool. Early, and the API may still change before 1.0. The core (scene tree, transforms, orthographic projection, depth sorting) and the SVG string renderer work and are tested. Not built yet: a canvas renderer, general animation, and framework bindings. The one animation available is a constant turn about one axis (see Turning in place ). npm install @zpup/core Zpup is ESM-only and has no runtime dependencies. It is built for ES2022 and tested on Node 24; it uses no Node APIs, so it also runs in browsers. Bundled and minified, the whole library is 69 KB (26 KB gzipped), and renderSvg alone is 50 KB (19 KB gzipped). A scene is a plain object tree. renderSvg turns it into an SVG string, with no DOM, so it works on a server and the first paint needs no JavaScript. Here is a pup built from thick dots and lines, renderSvg(pup) : A smaller scene: import { dot , ellipse , renderSvg } from '@zpup/core' ; const svg = renderSvg ( { width : 120 , height : 120 , rotate : { x : - 20 , y : 30 } , children : [ dot ( { stroke : 40 , color : '#e62' } ) , // a thick dot is a sphere ellipse ( { diameter : 70 , stroke : 5 , color : '#636' , rotate : { x : 90 } } ) , // a ring around it ] , } ) ; The helpers only add a type field, so the same scene can be written, stored and sent as JSON: { "width" : 120 , "height" : 120 , "rotate" : { "x" : -20 , "y" : 30 }, "children" : [ { "type" : " dot " , "stroke" : 40 , "color" : " #e62 " }, { "type" : " ellipse " , "diameter" : 70 , "stroke" : 5 , "color" : " #636 " , "rotate" : { "x" : 90 } } ] } To see the scene from another side, change rotate on the scene and render again. Nothing else in the scene has to change: const front = renderSvg ( { ... scene , rotate : { x : - 16 , y : 24 } } ) ; const back = renderSvg ( { ... scene , rotate : { x : - 16 , y : 204 } } ) ; const above = renderSvg ( { ... scene , rotate : { x : - 62 , y : 24 } } ) ; The basics Axes: x right, y down, z toward the viewer. The origin is the center of the image. Angles: degrees. Positive rotate.z turns clockwise on screen. Nodes: group , path , ellipse , rect , polygon , and the solids box , cylinder , cone and hemisphere . Every node takes translate , rotate , scale , visible and children ; children inherit their parent's transform. Shapes: color (hex, rgb() and other CSS functions, or one of the CSS color names; a misspelled name is an error), stroke (round-capped width; thick strokes give volume) and fill . Solids: box , pyramid , cylinder , cone and hemisphere , always filled. One color is enough: each face gets a fixed lighter or darker version of it by the direction it faces in the scene, so a box does not collapse into a flat hexagon. Face options such as topFace or frontFace set a face's exact color. As in Zdog, cylinders, cones and hemispheres point along z; rotate: { x: 90 } stands them up. A box and a pyramid stand upright as they are. Errors: an invalid scene or option throws a ZpupValidationError that lists every problem with its path, what was expected and how to fix it. Each issue has the path as a string ( path ) and as keys and indices ( pathSegments ), and the message with ( message ) and without ( detail ) the path in front. checkScene(scene) returns the same list without throwing. checkSceneWarnings(scene) lists things that are valid but probably unintended, such as angles in radians, shapes placed outside the image, or shapes of different colors that pass through each other. Solids The lighthouse is made of eleven solids, each with a single color, plus a door and a window drawn as rectangles on the tower: import { cone , cylinder } from '@zpup/core' ; const up = { x : 90 } ; // round solids point along z; this stands them up cylinder ( { diameter : 60 , length : 36 , rotate : up , color : '#f4f1ea' } ) ; // a band of the tower cone ( { diameter : 44 , length : 18 , rotate : up , color : '#d8463c' } ) ; // the hut's roof A pyramid stands on a rectangular base with its top straight above the middle. Its ridge turns the point into an edge, which gives the three usual roofs from one shape ( scene ): pyramid ( { width : 68 , depth : 52 , height : 30 } ) ; // a point pyramid ( { width : 68 , depth : 52 , height : 30 , ridge : 30 } ) ; // a hip roof pyramid ( { width : 68 , depth : 52 , height : 30 , ridge : 68 } ) ; // a gable roof, or a wedge Solids are depth-sorted like everything else, against each other and against flat shapes. Rest one solid on a flat face of another; solids that cut into each other cannot be drawn correctly. By default every shape has one flat color. shading: "soft" on the scene shades round things from their color, as if lit from the upper left: dots and the round surfaces of solids (the side of a cylinder or cone, the dome of a hemisphere) with a gradient, and thick lines as tubes. Flat shapes and lines stay as they are. renderSvg ( { width : 120 , height : 120 , shading : 'soft' , children : [ dot ( { stroke : 80 , color : '#e62' } ) ] , } ) ; The light belongs to the picture, not to the scene: it stays in the upper left when the view changes. In a turning picture, a ball keeps its shading all the way round, and so does the side of an upright cylinder or cone turning about the vertical axis. A side that is tilted changes direction on screen as it turns, and its shading follows in steps of 15 degrees. Shapes of the same color that cut into each other look like one shape when flat. With soft shading each has its own highlight, so the seam shows, and in a turning picture the moment one passes in front of the other shows too. Keep such shapes just touching, or leave the shading flat. A flat shape takes backface , as in Zdog: true (the default) draws it from both sides, false leaves it out while its front (its local +z side) faces away, and a color paints its back in that color. This is what keeps a turning character clean. Zpup paints whole shapes back to front, so an eye drawn as a dot on a head has to jump from in front of the head to behind it as the head turns, and it does so while it still covers part of the head: the eye flickers. Built this way instead, a model turns without popping: import { dot , ellipse , group } from '@zpup/core' ; const head = [ dot ( { stroke : 80 , color : '#f4c95d' } ) , group ( { rotate : { x : 15 , y : - 25 } , // points the eye's +z up and to the left children : [ ellipse ( { translate : { z : 40.5 } , width : 8 , height : 11 , fill : true , stroke : 0 , color : '#222' , backface : false , } ) , ] , } ) , ] ; Turning in place A scene can also be shown turning. renderSpinSvg returns an SVG that turns the scene one full rotation, forever, using SMIL animation. It needs no JavaScript, so it also plays inside an tag and in a GitHub README. It suits small scenes; the file grows quickly with the number of shapes (see the limits below). import { renderSpinSvg } from '@zpup/core' ; const svg = renderSpinSvg ( scene , { axis : 'y' , // which angle of scene.rotate turns: 'x', 'y' (default, a turntable) or 'z' duration : 8 , // seconds per turn keyframes : 36 , // exact angles per turn; the browser interpolates in between direction : 'positive' , // or 'negative' precision : 1 , // decimals kept in coordinates } ) ; Every option is optional, and bad values throw a ZpupValidationError like an invalid scene does. Renderers without SMIL show the first frame, which is the same picture renderSvg draws. The pictures on this page were checked in Chrome, Safari's engine (WebKit) and Firefox. It is synchronous and depth-sorts the scene at 720 angles: about 60 ms for a small scene and 0.6 s for the lighthouse on a laptop, so in a browser run it in a worker (the playground does). Limits: See docs/decisions.md for how it works. There is no perspective and no light to place, by design; soft shading is a fixed look, not a lighting model. See docs/decisions.md for the reasoning behind these and other choices, and llms.txt for a compact reference written for AI coding tools. @zpup/mcp is an MCP server that lets a model write a scene, get its mistakes back as errors that say where they are and how to fix them, and see a PNG of the picture from several angles in one call. { "mcpServers" : { "zpup" : { "command" : " npx " , "args" : [ " -y " , " @zpup/mcp " ] } } } A model that can run code needs only the library and llms.txt . Requires Node.js 22.18 or later (the example script runs TypeScript directly) and pnpm . pnpm install pnpm test # unit and snapshot tests pnpm typecheck pnpm lint pnpm build # writes dist/ pnpm example # writes the pictures in examples/ pnpm playground:build # builds the playground into playground/dist/, servable as static files The MCP server is a second package in mcp/ , built with pnpm --dir mcp build . Its tests run with the rest. Raise the version in package.json (and, for the server, in mcp/package.json and both places in mcp/server.json ), add the changes to the changelog, and push a tag: git tag v0.3.0 && git push origin v0.3.0 The release workflow then publishes whatever version is not out yet: @zpup/core and @zpup/mcp to npm, and the server's entry to the MCP Registry. It uses no tokens; npm trusts the workflow by name. A tag starting with mcp-v does the same, for a release of the server alone. Zpup is inspired by Zdog by David DeSandro. It is a new implementation that shares no code with Zdog. It is an independent project and is not affiliated with Zdog or Metafizzy. MIT
